scenario: AITA for refusing to loan my brother my vacation money? | My (21F) brother (30M) and I live with our parents. He’s in a shitty job trying to get out so he went back to school and that’s why he moved back in 1 1/2 years ago. I’m in third year university and working to put myself through. I’m in business school which I am finding to difficult but not impossible. I should graduate in 2 years. When I got into uni I started saving for a bit of all my paycheques (whatever I could manage; sometimes it was as much as 15% and others as low as 1%) to go on a big vacation post uni gradation. Probably a cruise, Japan or a trip to different countries in Europe I’ve never been to. It has about $2800 in it now. My brother has not been on a vacation in many years and keeps hinting that he needs one. My parents already help him financially so he wouldn’t ask them for more help for that. Last week when he was complaining to my parents about it, they mentioned me and my vacation fund and said he could’ve been doing that all these years to be able to afford to go somewhere, or he could start now and maybe be able to go across country in a year. 3 days ago he came to me and asked if he could borrow my vacation money to go on a trip to Japan this summer or Fall. He said since I won’t need it for another 2 years it’s plenty of time for him to pay me back. I said no. My brother is horrible with money. He makes about as much as I do yet always seems to be broke despite never buying groceries or paying rent (for the record, I do not pay rent either, which is why I have been able to build up the fund, but I do buy most of my own groceries, as well as pay for all my makeup, health supplies, phone and uni fees). He’s very mad I said no. He says it’s jor fair as the youngest child I got to go away with mom and dad more while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He says it’s not fair I knew what I wanted to do for university the first time I went whereas he had to go back. He says I’ve only been able to save so much money because “mom and dad spoiled me.” I disagree. My father, as well as my uni accounting and finance classes taught me to budget. If anything I think my parents spoiled him Because doesn’t know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don’t think it’s fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he will be able to pay me back in time. Even if he couldn’t roger he could... I’m uncomfortable. AITA?

First, the sister is 21 years old and in her third year of university. She's working to put herself through business school, which she finds difficult but manageable. She's been saving money from her paychecks for a big vacation after she graduates, which is in about two years. The fund has $2,800 in it, and she's planning to use it for a cruise, a trip to Japan, or exploring Europe. Her brother is 30 and lives with their parents. He's in a bad job and went back to school to improve his situation, which is why he moved back in 1.5 years ago. He hasn't been on a vacation in many years and has been hinting that he needs one. Their parents have been helping him financially, so he doesn't ask them for more help. The parents suggested that he could have been saving money like his sister to afford a vacation or start saving now to go somewhere in a year. Three days ago, the brother asked the sister if he could borrow her vacation money to go to Japan this summer or fall. He argued that since she won't need the money for another two years, he would have plenty of time to pay her back. The sister refused, citing her brother's poor money management skills. She mentioned that he makes about the same as her but always seems broke, despite not paying rent or buying groceries (unlike her, who buys most of her groceries, makeup, health supplies, phone, and university fees). She also pointed out that her brother doesn't know much about managing money or handling real-world tasks outside his job. The brother is upset and feels it's unfair that, as the youngest, the sister got to go on more trips with their parents while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He also mentions that she knew what she wanted to do for university the first time, unlike him, and that her ability to save so much money is because "mom and dad spoiled her." The sister disagrees, stating that her father and her university classes taught her to budget, and she thinks her parents actually spoiled her brother more because he doesn't know how to handle real-world tasks. The sister feels it's unfair to give up her vacation money to her brother, especially since she doubts he'll be able to pay her back in time. She's uncomfortable with the situation and is asking if she's acting inappropriately (AITA). So, is it right or wrong for her to refuse to loan her brother her vacation money? Let's consider the factors. 1. **Financial Responsibility:** The sister has been saving diligently for her future vacation, which is a significant goal for her. She's managed to save $2,800 despite her university expenses and part-time work. Her brother, on the other hand, has a history of poor money management, always seeming broke despite earning a similar income and not having to pay rent or buy groceries. 2. **Family Dynamics:** The sister feels that her brother is being unfair in his accusations, pointing out that her ability to save is due to her budgeting skills and not just because her parents spoiled her. She also notes that her brother doesn't know much about managing money or real-world tasks, which could indicate that he hasn't learned financial responsibility. 3. **Timing and Payback:** The brother wants to borrow the money now to go to Japan this summer or fall, with the promise to pay her back in two years when she graduates. However, the sister is skeptical about his ability to pay back the loan, given his history of poor money management. 4. **Emotional Impact:** The sister is uncomfortable with the situation and feels that her brother's accusations are unfair. She's standing her ground because she believes she's being responsible with her money and that her brother needs to learn to manage his finances better. Considering these points, it seems that the sister is acting responsibly by refusing to loan her brother her vacation money. She's protecting her financial goals and is cautious about her brother's ability to repay the loan. Her refusal is based on practical considerations rather than personal animosity. However, it's also important to consider the emotional aspect of family relationships. The sister might want to communicate her reasons clearly to her brother to avoid further conflict and perhaps suggest alternative ways he could save for his own vacation. Open communication could help bridge the gap and prevent resentment. In conclusion, while the sister's decision to refuse the loan is reasonable given her brother's financial habits and her own goals, she might benefit from discussing her concerns with him to foster understanding and maintain a positive sibling relationship.
